title: Replaying Evolution in Real Time
endLine: Replicate populations and archived ancestors turn evolution into a repeatable test.

scenes.tts: How can biologists test what drove evolution when history happened only once? Experimental evolution watches replicate populations change under controlled conditions. It also archives ancestors to compare past with present.
scenes.caption: How can biologists test what drove evolution when history happened only once? Experimental evolution watches replicate populations change under controlled conditions. It also archives ancestors to compare past with present.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on the carried lab benchtop world (schematic, fills 65% of frame height): a single faded fossil timeline cracks into a large question mark as the first question finishes. The timeline transforms into three lit glass flasks of drifting cells above a generation track, while glowing sample vials drop into an archive tray below labeled 'Past' and 'Present'. Ambient drifting cells keep the frame alive.
scenes.narration: How can biologists test what drove evolution when history happened only once? Experimental evolution watches replicate populations change under controlled conditions. It also archives ancestors to compare past with present.

scenes.visual: Carried benchtop world dims slightly while cells keep drifting slowly inside the flasks. The title 'Replaying Evolution in Real Time' fades in cleanly at center, holds briefly, and fades out as the flasks brighten.

scenes.tts: Split one genotype into replicate flasks differing in one factor. In 1998, Rainey and Travisano grew the bacterium Pseudomonas fluorescens in unshaken or shaken broth. Unshaken broth formed zones from the surface down, each a different way to live. New heritable types evolved there; in shaken flasks that diversity did not arise.
scenes.caption: Split one genotype into replicate flasks differing in one factor. In 1998, Rainey and Travisano grew the bacterium Pseudomonas fluorescens in unshaken or shaken broth. scenes.visual: Carried benchtop world (schematic): one starter flask of uniform cells pours into two matched groups of replicate flasks, labeled 'Unshaken' on the left and 'Shaken' on the right (1998, Rainey & Travisano). Before named, the unshaken flasks settle into shaded horizontal zones from the surface down as a surface mat and distinct coloured cell types emerge and gently drift; the shaken flasks swirl continuously with only the single ancestral cell colour.

scenes.tts: As generations pass, biologists freeze samples to revive later. Replicate populations and archived ancestors turn evolutionary history into an experiment you can repeat. When bacteria evolve with the phages infecting them, samples are paired across time. That cross is a time-shift assay.
scenes.caption: As generations pass, biologists freeze samples to revive later. Replicate populations and archived ancestors turn evolutionary history into an experiment you can repeat. When bacteria evolve with the phages infecting them, samples are paired across time. That cross is a time-shift assay.
scenes.visual: Carried benchtop world (schematic): a marker glides rightward along the generation track below the flasks. At regular ticks, paired vials of bacteria (circles) and phages (small triangles) drop into the chilled archive shelf below. As the guiding idea is spoken, the replicate flasks and archive shelf glow together. Then one vial of phages lifts from the middle time point and arrows link it to past, same-time and future host vials, forming a three-column 'Time-shift assay' test strip.
scenes.narration: As generations pass, biologists freeze samples to revive later. Replicate populations and archived ancestors turn evolutionary history into an experiment you can repeat. When bacteria evolve with the phages infecting them, samples are paired across time. That cross is a time-shift assay.

scenes.tts: Test phages from one week on past, same-time and future hosts. Without heritable change, every pairing gives similar infection. In an arms race, both sides escalate, so infection falls from past to future hosts. Under fluctuating selection, parasites track current hosts, so infection rises and falls in a wave.
scenes.caption: Test phages from one week on past, same-time and future hosts. Without heritable change, every pairing gives similar infection. In an arms race, both sides escalate, so infection falls from past to future hosts. Under fluctuating selection, parasites track current hosts, so infection rises and falls in a wave.
scenes.visual: Carried time-shift test strip expands cleanly into a schematic infection graph over the archive shelf, with x-axis 'Past', 'Same time', 'Future' hosts and y-axis 'Infection'. First, three equal bars settle into a flat line ('No change'). Next, the same line tilts downward from high on Past to low on Future ('Arms race'). Then the curve bends into a smooth rising-and-falling wave peaking at Same time ('Fluctuating selection'), with gentle motion along the curve.
scenes.narration: Test phages from one week on past, same-time and future hosts. Without heritable change, every pairing gives similar infection. In an arms race, both sides escalate, so infection falls from past to future hosts. Under fluctuating selection, parasites track current hosts, so infection rises and falls in a wave.

scenes.tts: Now try one. A lab samples a bacterium and its phage for twenty weeks. In the time-shift assay, infection falls steadily from past hosts to future ones. Can the lab conclude this is an arms race?
scenes.caption: Now try one. A lab samples a bacterium and its phage for 20 weeks. In the time-shift assay, infection falls steadily from past hosts to future ones. Can the lab conclude this is an arms race?
scenes.visual: Carried schematic graph clears to a narrow bracket labeled '20 weeks' on the time axis. Three points draw a steady downward slope from Past to Future hosts as the narrator describes the assay. Above the curve, a high-contrast question card settles: 'Arms race?'.
scenes.narration: Now try one. A lab samples a bacterium and its phage for 20 weeks. In the time-shift assay, infection falls steadily from past hosts to future ones. Can the lab conclude this is an arms race?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause: hold the schematic 20-week falling line and 'Arms race?' question on screen for 4.5 seconds while a quiet, minimal progress ring fills gently in the corner.

scenes.tts: Not yet. A short record can cover one falling slope of a wave and look like an arms race. Long, dense records with replicate lines tell them apart. Replicates also guard against drift, random change in small populations. Drift scatters lines, while selection pushes them the same way.

scenes.visual: Carried schematic graph zooms outward from the 20-week bracket: the short falling line reveals itself as one downward segment of a much longer rising-and-falling wave, densely dotted with samples. Below, three replicate trajectories appear: first drifting apart in random directions ('Drift'), then smoothly aligning into parallel tracks in one direction ('Selection'), with gentle ambient motion.

scenes.tts: Matched controls rule out shared lab or greenhouse effects. To separate coevolution from one-sided adaptation, Paterson and colleagues in 2010 held the host at one genotype. Even then, coevolution needs heritable change in both partners. And flasks test mechanisms, not field communities.
scenes.caption: Matched controls rule out shared lab or greenhouse effects. To separate coevolution from one-sided adaptation, Paterson and colleagues in 2010 held the host at one genotype. Even then, coevolution needs heritable change in both partners. And flasks test mechanisms, not field communities.
scenes.visual: Carried benchtop world returns (schematic): a matched control flask lights up beside the evolving flasks to cancel a glowing 'Shared room' backdrop. Next, two phage-host lines sit side by side (Paterson et al. 2010): in one, both host and phage colours shift; in the other, a lock icon holds the host colour fixed ('Constant host'). Finally, the flask shrinks gently beside a wide sunlit meadow silhouette labeled 'Field community' to show scope.
scenes.narration: Matched controls rule out shared lab or greenhouse effects. To separate coevolution from one-sided adaptation, Paterson and colleagues in 2010 held the host at one genotype. scenes.tts: What has this unlocked? In 2008, Blount, Borland and Lenski grew twelve identical Escherichia coli populations. Their medium held glucose and citrate the cells could not use. One evolved citrate use in oxygen by about generation thirty-one thousand five hundred. Replaying frozen clones showed later generations evolved it more often, suggesting earlier changes mattered.
scenes.caption: What has this unlocked? In 2008, Blount, Borland and Lenski grew twelve identical Escherichia coli populations. Their medium held glucose and citrate the cells could not use. One evolved citrate use in oxygen by about generation 31,500. Replaying frozen clones showed later generations evolved it more often, suggesting earlier changes mattered.
scenes.visual: Carried benchtop world (schematic): twelve identical flasks line the bench (Blount, Borland & Lenski 2008). The generation counter sweeps rapidly to '31,500', where one single flask shifts bright gold ('Citrate use') while eleven stay unchanged. Frozen vials lift from early and late spots in the archive shelf below and replay into fresh flasks: far more late-generation replays turn gold.

scenes.tts: Nature archives in pond mud. In 2007, Decaestecker and colleagues revived dormant Daphnia water-flea eggs and parasite spores from dated sediment layers. This resurrection ecology showed parasites adapted within a few years. Virulence, the harm to infected hosts, rose through time.
scenes.caption: Nature archives in pond mud. In 2007, Decaestecker and colleagues revived dormant Daphnia water-flea eggs and parasite spores from dated sediment layers. This resurrection ecology showed parasites adapted within a few years. Virulence, the harm to infected hosts, rose through time.
scenes.visual: The archive shelf at the bottom of the carried frame morphs into four dated horizontal pond-sediment layers beneath gently rippling water (schematic; Decaestecker et al. 2007). Dormant Daphnia eggs and tiny parasite spores rise from stacked layers into test dishes above. As layers pair across time, a schematic 'Virulence' gauge climbs steadily upward from older to younger layers.

scenes.tts: In 2017, Gervasi and Schiestl pollinated replicate field mustard populations by bumblebees, by hoverflies, or by hand. Hand pollination was the control. Nine generations later, compared at generation eleven, bumblebee lines were taller and hoverfly lines self-pollinated more. Replicates, controls and archived ancestors test evolution directly.

scenes.visual: Carried benchtop transforms into three neat groups of potted field mustard plants (schematic; Gervasi & Schiestl 2017), labeled 'Bumblebees', 'Hoverflies' and 'Hand control'. As a generation counter ticks from 1 to 9, bumblebee-pollinated plants grow visibly taller while hoverfly-pollinated flowers curl inward to self-pollinate, while the hand-pollinated control shows neither change. In the final beat, the flasks, sediment layers and plant replicates align cleanly above the glowing archive tray.
